meta.author: cursor-agent (stats draft for human flair pass)
meta.notes: Birth-weighted distributions from Statistics Estonia and TAI. Home place is sampled from curated town/district banks keyed by county + urban/rural. Childhood GP-visit beats cite probable causes (otitis, caries, ARI). School-mark patterns use Estonia's 5-point scale with PISA-informed SES bias. Later-life pools remain mostly color stubs for the flair pass. Birth parent-situation lines vary within SR55 marital buckets; maternal death ~5/100k (modeled MMR 2023); adoption kept scarce as color.

style_rules: No jargon (no 'modal path', 'quintile', 'stratum' in player text)
No life-expectancy numbers inside the story (those belong in About)
Prefer places, ages, and actions over abstract categories
Keep fact-tagged lines numerically honest even after flair edits
hard_nos: Do not invent county birth shares
Do not imply that color events are nationally representative
Avoid stigmatizing whole regions or ethnic groups
Do not put nationality/ethnicity into the birth opener by default

region.description: Mother's county of residence at birth; Tallinn split from Harju

source.notes: Live births by county, 2024. Tallinn from RV11U row "..Tallinn" (3262); harju_excl_tallinn = Harju county (4793) − Tallinn (3262) = 1531. Denominator = 9690 (Whole country). County-unknown = 0. Weights sum to 1.0.

class_level.description: Socioeconomic start for the birth story, proxied by mother's educational level at childbirth. Player-facing labels use class language; underlying ids map to pack education strata.

source.notes: Live births by mother's educational level, settlement total, age groups total. Below upper secondary 1185; upper secondary / post-secondary non-tertiary 3432; tertiary 5067. Unknown (6) excluded. Known total 9684.

parents_marital_status.description: Mother's marital status among women who gave birth (TAI Medical Birth Register)

source.notes: Women given birth, place of residence = Estonia, nationality = Total. Registered marriage 4375; cohabitation 4708; single 228; divorced 41; widow 2. Unknown (38) excluded. Known n = 9354 (all women = 9392 including unknown). Cross-check: Stat EE RV033 marital births = 46.64% in 2024 (https://andmed.stat.ee/en/stat/RV033).

settlement.description: Urban/rural settlement region of mother's residence at birth

mother_age_group.description: Mother's age group at childbirth (optional; not in default birth template)

mother_born_in.description: Mother's country of birth (optional; not in default birth template)

source.notes: Mother's country of birth, age groups total: Estonia 8429; foreign 1261 (EU except EE 120; non-EU 1141); unknown 0; total 9690.

mother_nationality.description: Mother's nationality among women who gave birth (TAI). Optional for conditional color later — do not put in the birth opener by default.

source.notes: Place of residence = Estonia. Estonian 6851; Russian 1564; other non-Estonian (Ukrainian 457 + Belarusian 24 + Finn 13 + Latvian 25 + other 456 = 975). Unknown (2) excluded. Known n = 9390. Labels are neutral facts for weighting — never use to stereotype regions.

school_marks.description: Typical report-card pattern on Estonia's 5-point scale (5 very good … 1 poor). Biased by class_level using PISA SES gap directionally.

values.label: marks drifting toward twos and ones

source.notes: Scale (exact): Estonian 5-point grades — 5 väga hea (90–100%), 4 hea (75–89%), 3 rahuldav (50–74%), 2 puudulik, 1 nõrk (Harno secondary-education factsheet; same scale used in basic school). Share of each report-card pattern is approximate (no national GPA census). Class bias is directional from PISA 2022 EE: advantaged vs disadvantaged maths gap 81 points; SES explains ~13% of maths variance (OECD country note).

beats.title: Birth
beats.template: Born in {region}, Estonia, into {class_level} family. You were born a {sex}. {parent_situation} Home was in {place}.
beats.notes: parent_situation is sampled from parent_situation_events, gated by rolled parents_marital_status (TAI SR55). Rare maternal-death / adoption lines are tiny weights.

beats.title: Early childhood
beats.notes: One concrete happening. Prefer color until more childhood stats are wired.

early_childhood_events.text: you were still growing up in {place}.
early_childhood_events.notes: Continuity assumption; not a migration statistic.

early_childhood_events.text: a middle-ear infection kept sending you back to the family doctor between kindergarten mornings.

source.publisher: Global Burden of Disease / pediatric literature
source.notes: Otitis media is among the most common childhood illnesses worldwide and a leading reason for pediatric primary-care visits; used here as a high-prior childhood GP visit cause. Estonia-specific AOM incidence is not published as a clean national rate — confidence approximate.

early_childhood_events.text: the dentist found cavities — common in Estonian preschoolers — so family-doctor week suddenly included dental visits too.

source.notes: Study of Estonian 2–4-year-olds: caries in ~42% (dmft mean 1.6). Older study; still a documented EE childhood burden.

early_childhood_events.text: a winter cough and runny nose that would not clear meant repeat family-doctor visits while kindergarten still expected you each morning.

source.notes: Acute respiratory infections are routinely the largest block of communicable-disease surveillance in Estonia and heavily affect preschool cohorts; exact visit rates vary by season/year.

early_childhood_events.text: a younger sibling arrived and the flat in {place} felt suddenly smaller.
grandparents covered long stretches of childcare in {place} while the adults worked.

early_childhood_events.notes: Aftermath wording is color variety; move A→B places stay concrete.

school_events.text: you were in basic school near {place}, {school_year_texture}.
the trip from {place} to school ate a chunk of every morning — {school_trip_texture}.
around {place}, the stairwell mixed Estonian and Russian depending on who was shouting.
school_events.notes: Color only. Do not treat as a language-statistics claim.

school_events.text: your report card showed {school_marks}, and adults talked about what comes after school as if the path were already drawn.

source.notes: Uses rolled school_marks (5-point scale + PISA SES-biased weights).

school_events.text: with {school_marks} on the report card, teachers mentioned vocational options more often than university brochures.

leaving_school_events.text: you finished secondary school and had to choose earning versus more study.
you took a vocational route — workshop hours, a practical certificate, a clearer job door.
university applications were the expected next step, not a surprise.
paid work pulled harder than the timetable, and school slipped down the list.

early_work_events.text: you had a first formal job with a contract, a supervisor, and a pay day you could count on.
shifts ran long and the body learned the job before the CV did.
you started behind a desk where everyone seemed to have a degree and an opinion.

family_events.text: you moved in with a partner and learned how quickly rent eats a month.
the first child arrived before either of you felt fully ready on paper.
you timed family around two careers that did not pause politely.

midlife_events.text: life looked ordinary from the outside — work, home, the quiet math of staying afloat.
doctor visits started using longer words than they used to.
the children were old enough to ignore you and still young enough to need you.

parent_situation_events.text: Your mother and father had only recently married.
parent_situation_events.notes: Color timing within marriage; not a national newlywed-at-birth rate.

parent_situation_events.text: Your parents had been married for years before you arrived.
Your parents had been married for about fifteen years when you were born.
parent_situation_events.notes: Color duration; mean mother age ~31 leaves room for long prior marriages but exact share unknown.

parent_situation_events.text: Your mother was married, and home already had the quiet routines of a long household.
Your mother was living together unmarried with your father.
Your parents shared a home but had not put marriage on paper.
Your mother and father lived together and talked about marrying later.
Your parents were a couple without a wedding date — ordinary enough in Estonia.

source.notes: Cohabitation is the plurality marital status among women giving birth in Estonia (SR55 2024).

parent_situation_events.text: Your mother was a single mother.
Your mother was on her own — your father had left before you learned his face.
Your mother raised the start of your life without a partner named on the forms.
Your mother was single; the man who might have been your father had already disappeared from the story.
Your mother was divorced when you were born.
Your mother was divorced, and your father lived elsewhere from the start.
Your mother was widowed when you were born.
Your father had died before you arrived; your mother began alone.
Your mother died in childbirth; your father was left to raise you.

source.notes: Estonia maternal mortality ~5 deaths per 100,000 live births (2023 modeled). Extremely rare by design.

parent_situation_events.text: You were adopted early; the adults who raised you were not the ones who gave birth to you.
parent_situation_events.notes: Color/rare — Estonia domestic adoption at birth is uncommon; not a published birth-register share. Keep scarce.

move_aftermath_events.text: and you had to say goodbye to your old friends
and you made new friends quickly
and you did not have any friends to miss
and your only friends were your parents and siblings anyway
and you felt alone in the new place for a long time
and you were excited to see new places
and the new courtyard stayed quiet for weeks before anyone asked your name
and you missed your old room more than anyone admitted
and the adults treated it like an adventure even when you did not
and you started over shy, watching the other kids from the edge

school_year_texture_events.text: measuring the year in bus stops and term tests
learning every crack in the schoolyard asphalt
counting down to weekends more carefully than to holidays
with the same coat hook and the same drafty window all year
where lunch smelled the same every day and the bell still surprised you
keeping score in friendships as carefully as in marks
and the walk home was half the education
with chalkboard dust on your sleeves by noon
mostly from the quiet back row unless someone called your name
hauling gym shoes in a plastic bag that never quite closed

school_trip_texture_events.text: fog on the bus windows and wet wool in the aisle
and one missed connection meant a late mark

example_rolls.title: tallinn_tertiary_cohab
example_rolls.output: Born in Tallinn, Estonia, into an upper-middle-class family. You were born a girl. Your parents shared a home but had not put marriage on paper. Home was in Kadriorg in Tallinn. When you were 3, a middle-ear infection kept sending you back to the family doctor between kindergarten mornings. At 12, your report card showed mostly fours and fives, and adults talked about what comes after school as if the path were already drawn.

example_rolls.title: ida_viru_working_married_boy
example_rolls.output: Born in Ida-Viru county, Estonia, into a working-class family. You were born a boy. Your parents had been married for years before you arrived. Home was in Narva. When you were 4, grandparents covered long stretches of childcare in Narva while the adults worked. At 14, with threes with some twos on the report card, teachers mentioned vocational options more often than university brochures.

example_rolls.title: viljandi_middle_rural_move
example_rolls.output: Born in Viljandi county, Estonia, into a middle-class family. You were born a girl. Your parents had been married for years before you arrived. Home was in Suure-Jaani. When you were 5, your family moved from Suure-Jaani to Annelinn in Tartu, and you were excited to see new places. At 11, the trip from Annelinn in Tartu to school ate a chunk of every morning — rain, ice, or sun.

llm_brief.goal: Implement a life-path generator for Estonia that rolls the fact variables from this file, walks beats until age-at-death, and composes text from templates + pools. Wire class_level to existing education strata in data/countries/EST.json.
must: Keep 2024 weights unless updating with a newer cited year
Reuse vocab/pack stratum ids: below-upper-secondary, upper-secondary, tertiary
Cite RV11U, RV106, RV142U, RV115, SR55 (and RV033 as cross-check) in country pack sources
Preserve mother-based marital wording unless a better two-parent source is added
Roll mother_age_group / mother_born_in / mother_nationality but keep them out of birth template by default
must_not: Hardcode only a few full stories per class
Put nationality into the birth opener without an explicit design decision
deliverables: Generator wiring + sample outputs in the PR
